title: CMS Nursing Facility Requirements of Participation — Key Standards
chunks: CMS Requirements of Participation (RoP) for Long-Term Care Facilities — Overview. The CMS Requirements of Participation (42 CFR Part 483, Subpart B) establish the health and safety standards that Medicare and Medicaid-certified nursing facilities must meet. Facilities that fail to meet these standards may be subject to civil monetary penalties, denial of payment, or termination from the Medicare/Medicaid program.

Resident Rights (42 CFR §483.10). Each resident has the right to: be treated with dignity and respect; receive adequate and appropriate care; be free from abuse, neglect, and exploitation; make choices about care; receive visitors; manage their own finances; and have privacy. Facilities must inform residents of their rights in writing and in a language they understand.

Freedom from Abuse, Neglect, and Exploitation (42 CFR §483.12). Facilities must develop and implement written policies to prohibit abuse, neglect, misappropriation, and exploitation. All alleged violations must be reported immediately to the administrator and appropriate state agencies. Staff must be trained on recognizing and preventing abuse.

Quality of Life (42 CFR §483.24). The facility must provide care and services to attain or maintain the highest practicable physical, mental, and psychosocial well-being of each resident. This includes activities, social services, and an environment that promotes dignity.

Quality of Care (42 CFR §483.25). The facility must ensure each resident receives the necessary care and services to attain or maintain the highest practicable physical, mental, and psychosocial well-being, consistent with the resident's comprehensive assessment and plan of care. Key areas include: pressure injuries, nutrition, hydration, vision and hearing, range of motion, urinary incontinence, and medication management.

Nursing Services (42 CFR §483.35). The facility must have sufficient nursing staff, including a Registered Nurse (RN) for at least 8 consecutive hours per day, 7 days per week. A Director of Nursing (DON) must be a licensed RN on a full-time basis. Staffing must be sufficient to meet the needs of residents.

Food and Nutrition Services (42 CFR §483.60). The facility must provide each resident with a nourishing, palatable, well-balanced diet that meets the daily nutritional and special dietary needs of each resident, taking into account the resident's needs and preferences. A qualified dietitian must be employed or on retainer.

Infection Prevention and Control (42 CFR §483.80). Facilities must establish and maintain an Infection Prevention and Control Program (IPCP) designed to provide a safe, sanitary, and comfortable environment and to help prevent the development and transmission of communicable diseases and infections. An Infection Preventionist must be designated and trained.

Physical Environment (42 CFR §483.90). The facility must be designed, constructed, equipped, and maintained to protect the health and safety of residents, personnel, and the public. Rooms must meet minimum space requirements. Emergency power must be available for essential systems.

Administration (42 CFR §483.70). The facility must be administered in a manner that enables it to use its resources effectively and efficiently to attain or maintain the highest practicable physical, mental, and psychosocial well-being of each resident. The governing body is legally responsible for all policies and operations.

Comprehensive Person-Centered Care Planning (42 CFR §483.21). The facility must develop a baseline care plan within 48 hours of admission and a comprehensive person-centered care plan within 7 days of the completion of the comprehensive assessment. The care plan must be developed with the resident and their representative.

Pharmacy Services (42 CFR §483.45). The facility must provide pharmaceutical services, including procedures to assure the accurate acquiring, receiving, dispensing, and administering of all drugs and biologicals. A pharmacist must review each resident's drug regimen at least monthly and report irregularities.

title: OSHA Healthcare Worker Safety — Bloodborne Pathogens and Infection Control
chunks: OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard (29 CFR 1910.1030). Employers in healthcare settings must implement an Exposure Control Plan (ECP) to minimize employee exposure to bloodborne pathogens such as HIV, Hepatitis B (HBV), and Hepatitis C (HCV). The ECP must be updated annually and available to all employees.

Universal Precautions. All human blood and certain body fluids are treated as if known to be infectious for HIV, HBV, and other bloodborne pathogens. Engineering controls (sharps disposal containers, needleless systems), work practice controls, and personal protective equipment (PPE) must be used to reduce exposure risk.

Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) in Healthcare. Healthcare workers must use appropriate PPE including gloves, gowns, face masks, eye protection, and face shields when there is anticipated exposure to blood or body fluids. Employers must provide PPE at no cost to employees. PPE must be removed before leaving the work area.

Hepatitis B Vaccination. Employers must make the Hepatitis B vaccine available to all employees who have occupational exposure to blood or body fluids, at no cost to the employee, within 10 working days of initial assignment to work where exposure may occur. Employees who decline must sign a declination form.

Post-Exposure Follow-Up. After an exposure incident (needlestick, splash to mucous membranes), the employer must provide a confidential medical evaluation and follow-up including documentation of the route of exposure, identification of the source individual (if feasible), and testing of the source individual's blood.

OSHA Hazard Communication Standard (29 CFR 1910.1200). Healthcare employees who work with hazardous chemicals (cleaning products, disinfectants, sterilants) must be trained on chemical hazards. Safety Data Sheets (SDS) must be readily available for all hazardous chemicals in the workplace.

Ergonomics and Safe Patient Handling. Healthcare workers are at high risk for musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) from patient handling. OSHA recommends implementing a Safe Patient Handling and Mobility (SPHM) program, using mechanical lift equipment, and training staff on proper body mechanics to reduce back injuries.

Workplace Violence Prevention in Healthcare. Healthcare workers face a significant risk of workplace violence. OSHA recommends facilities implement a Workplace Violence Prevention Program including: management commitment, worksite analysis, hazard prevention and control, safety and health training, and record-keeping.

N95 Respirators and Respiratory Protection. When caring for patients with suspected or confirmed airborne infectious diseases (tuberculosis, COVID-19), healthcare workers must use NIOSH-approved N95 or higher respirators. Employers must implement a written Respiratory Protection Program (29 CFR 1910.134) including fit testing and medical evaluation.

Recordkeeping and Reporting (29 CFR 1904). Employers with 10 or more employees must maintain records of work-related injuries and illnesses using OSHA Form 300 (Log), Form 300A (Summary), and Form 301 (Incident Report). Severe injuries (hospitalization, amputation, loss of eye) must be reported to OSHA within 24 hours.

title: CDC Infection Prevention in Long-Term Care Facilities
source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
chunks: CDC Core Infection Prevention Practices for Long-Term Care. Long-term care facilities (LTCFs) should implement core infection prevention practices to protect residents and healthcare workers. These include: hand hygiene, standard and transmission-based precautions, injection safety, environmental cleaning, and antibiotic stewardship.

Hand Hygiene in Long-Term Care. Hand hygiene is the single most important measure to prevent healthcare-associated infections (HAIs). Staff must perform hand hygiene before and after resident contact, before putting on and after removing gloves, and after contact with environmental surfaces near residents. Use alcohol-based hand rub (ABHR) or soap and water.

Standard Precautions. Standard precautions apply to all residents regardless of their suspected or confirmed infection status. Components include: hand hygiene, use of PPE (gloves, gowns, masks, eye protection), safe injection practices, respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette, and proper handling of contaminated equipment.

Transmission-Based Precautions. In addition to standard precautions, transmission-based precautions are used for residents with suspected or confirmed infections spread by contact, droplet, or airborne routes. Contact precautions (gown and gloves) are used for MRSA, C. diff, and norovirus. Droplet precautions are used for influenza, COVID-19, and RSV.

COVID-19 in Long-Term Care Facilities. LTCFs must follow current CDC guidance for COVID-19 prevention, which includes vaccination of staff and residents, surveillance for COVID-like illness, cohorting strategies, visitation policies, and reporting to public health. Facilities should have written response plans for COVID-19 outbreaks.

Influenza Prevention and Control. Annual influenza vaccination is recommended for all LTCF residents and staff. Facilities should have policies for early identification and management of influenza-like illness, antiviral prophylaxis and treatment, and outbreak investigation and reporting.

Clostridium difficile (C. diff) Prevention. C. diff is a leading cause of HAIs in LTCFs. Prevention measures include: hand hygiene with soap and water (ABHR is not effective against C. diff spores), contact precautions, environmental cleaning with EPA-approved sporicidal disinfectants, and antibiotic stewardship to reduce unnecessary antibiotic use.

MRSA Prevention in Long-Term Care. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is common in LTCFs. Key prevention strategies include: active surveillance cultures, contact precautions for MRSA-positive residents, hand hygiene, decolonization protocols, and environmental cleaning and disinfection.

Antibiotic Stewardship in Nursing Homes. CMS requires all nursing homes to have an antibiotic stewardship program. Key components include: policies for appropriate antibiotic use, tracking antibiotic prescribing data, reporting antibiotic use and resistance, educating staff and residents/families about antibiotic stewardship.

Outbreak Investigation and Reporting. LTCFs must have policies for detecting, investigating, and reporting outbreaks of infectious diseases. An outbreak is generally defined as more cases than expected. Facilities must report outbreaks of certain diseases to their local or state health department.

Urinary Tract Infection (UTI) Prevention. UTIs are one of the most common HAIs in LTCFs. Prevention measures include: avoiding unnecessary urinary catheterization, using aseptic technique for catheter insertion, maintaining a closed drainage system, removing catheters as soon as clinically indicated, and conducting regular surveillance for catheter-associated UTIs (CAUTIs).

Wound and Pressure Injury Infection Prevention. Residents in LTCFs are at high risk for pressure injuries (bed sores). Prevention includes: regular skin assessments, repositioning every 2 hours, appropriate support surfaces, nutritional support, and moisture management. Infected wounds require proper wound care and, when indicated, antimicrobial treatment.

title: CNA and Nursing Aide Scope of Practice and Responsibilities
source: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN) / CMS
chunks: Certified Nursing Assistant (CNA) Role Overview. CNAs work under the supervision of licensed nurses (RN or LPN) to provide direct care to residents in long-term care facilities. CNAs are responsible for assisting residents with activities of daily living (ADLs), monitoring and reporting changes in resident condition, and supporting residents' dignity and independence.

Activities of Daily Living (ADLs). CNAs assist residents with bathing, dressing, grooming, oral hygiene, toileting, ambulation, and eating. Care must be provided in a way that maintains the resident's dignity and promotes maximum independence. CNAs must follow each resident's individualized care plan when providing ADL assistance.

Vital Signs Monitoring. CNAs are responsible for measuring and recording vital signs including temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation (SpO2). CNAs must report any abnormal vital signs to the supervising nurse immediately. Normal adult ranges: Temperature 97–99°F, Pulse 60–100 bpm, Respirations 12–20/min, Blood Pressure 90–120/60–80 mmHg.

Reporting and Documentation. CNAs must promptly report any changes in a resident's condition to the supervising nurse, including changes in behavior, appetite, skin condition, pain level, or vital signs. Documentation of care provided must be accurate, timely, and complete. CNAs should never document care that was not provided.

Infection Control Responsibilities of CNAs. CNAs play a critical role in infection prevention by performing hand hygiene before and after resident contact, wearing appropriate PPE, following standard and transmission-based precautions, properly disposing of contaminated items, and reporting signs of infection in residents to the supervising nurse.

Patient/Resident Rights and CNA Responsibilities. CNAs must treat all residents with dignity and respect, maintain resident privacy and confidentiality, assist residents in exercising their rights, and report any suspected abuse, neglect, or exploitation immediately to the charge nurse and supervisor. All residents have the right to be free from abuse.

CNA Certification and Training Requirements. Federal law (OBRA '87) requires CNAs working in Medicare/Medicaid-certified nursing homes to complete a state-approved training program of at least 75 hours and pass a competency evaluation. CNAs must maintain active certification through continuing education and periodic competency evaluations.

Safe Mobility and Transfer Techniques. CNAs must use proper body mechanics and mechanical lift equipment to safely transfer and reposition residents, preventing injury to both the resident and the CNA. Gait belts should be used during ambulation assistance. CNAs must follow the resident's care plan for specific transfer instructions.

Nutritional Support Responsibilities. CNAs assist residents with meals, monitor food and fluid intake, report changes in appetite or eating difficulties, encourage adequate fluid intake to prevent dehydration, and accurately document intake as required. CNAs must recognize signs of aspiration and dysphagia and report these to the supervising nurse.

title: HIPAA Privacy and Security in Healthcare Settings
source: U.S. Department of Health & Human Services (HHS)
chunks: HIPAA Overview. The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) of 1996 establishes national standards to protect individuals' medical records and other personally identifiable health information (PHI). The Privacy Rule, Security Rule, and Breach Notification Rule are the three primary components of HIPAA relevant to healthcare workers.

Protected Health Information (PHI). PHI is any individually identifiable health information held or transmitted by a covered entity or business associate in any form. PHI includes names, addresses, dates, phone numbers, Social Security numbers, diagnoses, treatment information, and any other information that could identify a patient. PHI must be safeguarded at all times.

Minimum Necessary Standard. When using or disclosing PHI, covered entities must make reasonable efforts to limit PHI to the minimum necessary to accomplish the intended purpose. This means employees should only access PHI that is needed to perform their job duties. Curiosity about a patient's information is not a valid reason to access their records.

Permitted Disclosures of PHI. PHI may be disclosed without patient authorization for: treatment (sharing information with other treating providers), payment (billing insurers), and healthcare operations (quality improvement, staff training). PHI may also be disclosed for public health activities, reporting abuse, and law enforcement in limited circumstances.

Patient Rights Under HIPAA. Patients have the right to: access their own health records; request corrections to their records; receive an accounting of disclosures; request restrictions on certain uses of their PHI; receive confidential communications; and receive a Notice of Privacy Practices.

HIPAA Security Rule. The Security Rule requires covered entities to implement administrative, physical, and technical safeguards to protect electronic PHI (ePHI). This includes access controls, audit controls, integrity controls, and transmission security. All employees with access to ePHI must receive security awareness training.

Breach Notification Rule. A breach of PHI must be reported to affected individuals within 60 days of discovery. Breaches affecting 500 or more individuals in a state must also be reported to the Secretary of HHS and prominent media outlets. Healthcare workers who discover or suspect a breach must report it immediately to their privacy officer.

HIPAA Penalties. Penalties for HIPAA violations range from $100 to $50,000 per violation (with an annual cap of $1.5 million), depending on the level of negligence. Criminal penalties can include fines and imprisonment. Healthcare workers who knowingly disclose PHI without authorization may face termination and criminal prosecution.

Social Media and HIPAA. Healthcare workers must never post patient information, photos, or identifying details on social media, even with good intentions. Posting a photo of a patient without explicit written authorization is a HIPAA violation. Workers should also avoid discussing patient cases in public areas or with family/friends.

Business Associate Agreements. Vendors and service providers who handle PHI on behalf of a covered entity (including EHR vendors, billing companies, and IT support providers) must sign a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) before accessing PHI. The BAA establishes the permitted uses of PHI and requires appropriate safeguards.

title: Dementia Care and Alzheimer's Disease — Best Practices for Long-Term Care Staff
chunks: Understanding Dementia in Long-Term Care. Dementia is a general term for memory loss and other cognitive impairments severe enough to interfere with daily life. Alzheimer's disease accounts for 60–80% of dementia cases. In long-term care settings, a large proportion of residents have some form of dementia. Staff must understand how dementia affects behavior and communication.

Person-Centered Dementia Care. Person-centered care recognizes the uniqueness of each person with dementia. Key principles include: knowing the person's life history, preferences, and values; involving the person in decisions to the extent possible; focusing on remaining abilities rather than deficits; and providing emotional support and meaningful engagement.

Communication Strategies for Residents with Dementia. When communicating with a resident who has dementia: approach from the front and make eye contact; use simple, clear sentences; speak slowly and calmly; use the resident's name; avoid arguing or correcting; use positive body language; allow adequate time for responses; and use non-verbal communication such as touch (when appropriate).

Managing Behavioral and Psychological Symptoms of Dementia (BPSD). BPSD includes agitation, wandering, aggression, sundowning, and depression. Non-pharmacological approaches are preferred as first-line treatment: identify and address triggers; use redirection and distraction; provide structured activities; ensure adequate pain management; and maintain consistent routines.

Preventing and Responding to Wandering. Wandering is common in residents with dementia and poses a safety risk. Prevention strategies include: door alarms and secured exits, monitoring devices (WanderGuard), visual cues to redirect residents, safe walking areas, and regular activity programs to reduce restlessness. If a resident is found wandering, approach calmly and use gentle redirection.

Mealtime Challenges in Dementia Care. Residents with dementia may have difficulty eating due to forgetting how to use utensils, difficulty recognizing food, swallowing problems, or behavioral issues. Staff should: sit at eye level, offer foods one at a time, use finger foods if helpful, provide verbal and physical cues, monitor for signs of aspiration, and document food intake.

Pain Assessment in Residents with Dementia. Residents with advanced dementia may be unable to self-report pain. Staff should use behavioral pain assessment tools (e.g., PAINAD scale) and watch for non-verbal signs of pain: facial grimacing, guarding, agitation, changes in behavior, moaning, or resistance to care. Report suspected pain to the supervising nurse.

Sundowning. Sundowning refers to increased confusion, agitation, or restlessness that occurs in the late afternoon or evening in some residents with dementia. Management strategies include: maintaining consistent routines, providing adequate daytime activity and light exposure, reducing stimulation in the evening, and ensuring the resident is comfortable and not in pain.

title: Workplace Safety and Emergency Procedures in Long-Term Care
chunks: Fire Safety in Long-Term Care Facilities. Staff must know the facility's fire evacuation plan and their assigned roles. In the event of a fire: Rescue any residents in immediate danger; Activate the fire alarm; Contain the fire by closing doors; Extinguish the fire if safe to do so; Evacuate the area. Remember the RACE acronym: Rescue, Alarm, Contain, Extinguish/Evacuate.

Fire Extinguisher Use — PASS Technique. To use a fire extinguisher: Pull the pin; Aim the nozzle at the base of the fire; Squeeze the handle; Sweep side to side. Fire extinguishers are only appropriate for small, contained fires. Never use an elevator during a fire emergency. Assist residents to safety via stairwells using transfer devices.

Emergency Codes in Healthcare Facilities. Common emergency codes include: Code Red (Fire); Code Blue (Medical Emergency/Cardiac Arrest); Code White (Aggressive Person/Security); Code Silver (Person with Weapon); Code Green (Evacuation); Code Orange (Hazardous Materials). Staff must know all codes used in their facility.

Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) and DNR Orders. All direct care staff in long-term care should be trained in CPR. Before initiating CPR, verify the resident's code status. Residents with a Do-Not-Resuscitate (DNR) or Do-Not-Attempt-Resuscitation (DNAR) order should not receive CPR. POLST (Physician Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment) forms also guide emergency care decisions.

Hazardous Materials (HAZMAT) Safety. Staff who work with hazardous chemicals must be trained in safe handling, storage, and disposal. In case of a chemical spill: evacuate the area, notify the supervisor, consult the Safety Data Sheet (SDS) for the substance, and follow facility protocols for containment and cleanup. Never mix bleach with ammonia-based cleaners.

Back Safety and Injury Prevention. Back injuries are the leading occupational injury in healthcare. To prevent back injuries: use proper body mechanics (bend at the knees, not the waist); use mechanical lift equipment for resident transfers; ask for help when needed; maintain a healthy weight and exercise regularly; and report any back pain or injuries to your supervisor promptly.

Reporting Workplace Injuries. All workplace injuries, no matter how minor, must be reported to the supervisor and documented on an incident report immediately. Prompt reporting ensures proper medical treatment and helps identify hazards to prevent future injuries. Failure to report injuries may result in loss of workers' compensation benefits.

Severe Weather and Disaster Preparedness. Facilities must have emergency preparedness plans for severe weather (tornadoes, hurricanes, blizzards), power outages, and other disasters. Staff should know: shelter-in-place locations, backup power systems, emergency supply locations, communication procedures, and evacuation routes.
